title: Qubits
intro: The two-level system that every QRC spin reservoir is made of: its geometry on the Bloch sphere, the Pauli operators that measure and rotate it, interference, the gates and circuits that run reservoirs on quantum computers, and the pulses that make those gates on real hardware.

blocks.text: A qubit is the simplest quantum system that is not classical: a system with exactly two distinguishable states, $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$, that can also be in any superposition $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$. Real qubits are spin-1/2 nuclei (NMR), two levels of an atom or ion, or two levels of a superconducting circuit. The mathematics is the same for all of them, and once you know it you can follow almost everything a quantum computer, or a quantum reservoir, does.

The chapter builds that mathematics in five steps. First a picture: every qubit state is a point on a sphere. Then the operators that measure and rotate it. Then interference, the effect that makes quantum probabilities differ from classical ones: amplitudes for different routes add, and can cancel. Then the gates and circuits that combine qubits, including the CNOT that entangles them. Finally the physics underneath: how a real qubit is rotated by a pulse of microwaves or light.

Why it matters for this library. A quantum reservoir is a set of interacting qubits driven by an input. Every operation in one, writing the input in, letting the qubits interact, reading them out, is one of the things this chapter teaches you to compute by hand: a rotation, a coupling built from gates or a Hamiltonian, and a measurement whose odds you can read off the Bloch sphere.

You should be comfortable with complex numbers, kets and inner products, and the Born rule: the Foundations chapter (#/quantum/foundations), in particular States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation) and Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement). Nothing else is assumed.
Read them in this order; each page uses the one before it.

items: The Qubit and the Bloch Sphere (#/quantum/qubits/bloch-sphere): why a qubit state needs only two real numbers once normalisation and the unmeasurable global phase are taken out, and how they become the angles $\theta$ and $\varphi$ of a point on a sphere. It shows that the point's coordinates are the three expectation values $\langle X\rangle$, $\langle Y\rangle$, $\langle Z\rangle$, how to read measurement probabilities and overlaps straight off the picture (opposite points are orthogonal states), where the input state of a quantum reservoir sits, and a first look at mixed states inside the ball.

Pauli Operators and Rotations (#/quantum/qubits/pauli-and-rotations): the Pauli matrices $X$, $Y$, $Z$ as observables and as gates at the same time, how they multiply, the spin operator along any axis, and the key derivation of the chapter: why $e^{-i\theta P/2}$ rotates the Bloch sphere by $\theta$. It explains the half angle (a $360°$ turn multiplies a state by $-1$), why the order of rotations matters, how every single-qubit gate is three rotations (the Z-Y-Z decomposition), and the rotation that writes a number into a qubit.

Interference of Amplitudes (#/quantum/qubits/interference): the one rule behind quantum interference, that amplitudes for different routes add and can cancel. It follows amplitudes route by route through two Hadamards and through a Mach–Zehnder interferometer, computes the fringe and its visibility, shows how a record of which path was taken destroys the pattern (and how a quantum eraser brings it back), and ends with Deutsch's algorithm, the first example of a quantum computer winning by interference.

Gates and Circuits (#/quantum/qubits/gates-and-circuits): reading a circuit diagram as a product of matrices, the standard gates ($X$, $Z$, $H_d$, $S$, $T$) acting on amplitudes, gate identities and how to prove them, two-qubit states and the CNOT, the Bell circuit and the product test for entanglement, an $XX$ coupling built from two CNOTs, Trotter steps that turn a whole Hamiltonian into a circuit, universality, and what gate count and depth cost on real hardware.

Driven Qubits and Rabi Oscillations (#/quantum/qubits/driven-qubits): the physics underneath the gates. A qubit in a static field precesses; a weak drive at the qubit's own frequency, seen from a rotating frame with the rotating-wave approximation, rotates it. The page derives Rabi's formula on and off resonance, turns it into $\pi$ and $\pi/2$ pulses, explains the Ramsey experiment that measures a qubit's frequency, and describes how NMR, superconducting, trapped-ion and neutral-atom qubits are controlled.

blocks.text: How the pages fit together. The first two pages are the geometry: a state is a point and a gate is a rotation of the sphere. The third shows why phases, which the sphere draws as the azimuth $\varphi$, decide what you measure once paths recombine. The fourth adds a second qubit, where the new ingredient is entanglement, and turns everything into the language of circuits. The fifth goes back to a single qubit and asks how a rotation is physically made, which closes the loop: the rotations of the second page are the Rabi pulses of the fifth.
The key equations of the chapter

blocks.caption: Every pure qubit state, up to a global phase: a point at polar angle θ and azimuth φ on the Bloch sphere.
The height of the point on the sphere gives the measurement probabilities; the azimuth plays no part until another gate turns it into height.
A rotation by angle θ about the axis of the Pauli operator P; every single-qubit gate is a product of these, up to a global phase.
The Mach–Zehnder fringe: a relative phase φ between two paths, invisible on its own, decides the odds once the paths recombine.
The controlled-NOT: flip the target when the control is 1. With single-qubit gates it can build any circuit.
Rabi's formula: how a drive of strength Ω and detuning δ moves population from |0⟩ to |1⟩.

blocks.text: Each page takes one to two hours of careful reading if you work the 'Check yourself' questions as you go, which is the point of them, plus another hour for the problems at the end. The interactive Bloch sphere and circuit sandbox are worth time of their own: predict what a setting will do, then check.

The Dynamics chapter (#/quantum/dynamics) explains the evolution $e^{-iHt}$ that the gates here are special cases of, and the Many Qubits chapter (#/quantum/many-body) takes the two-qubit states met here to many qubits, entanglement and mixed states. On the QRC shelf, every spin reservoir is a network of the qubits described here, and Gate-Based Devices (#/qrc/hardware/gate-based-devices) runs one with the circuits of this chapter.
